newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Mexican retail slump tempers GDP euphoria.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mexican retail slump tempers GDP euphoria.

text.p: High debt levels and low wages in late 1996 continued to keep Mexicans out of the shops, puncturing some of the euphoria over the sharp fourth quarter rebound in economic growth, economists said on Friday.

"There is a weakness in consumption," said Alfredo Thorne, economist at J.P. Morgan in Mexico City. "If anyone has money in this economy, its middle to high earners. We know what's happened to low wage earners."

Indeed, he and other economists are pointing to a pattern of falling real wages, especially among the lowest paid, to explain why they believe a lingering slump in retail sales reported on Thursday tells the true story of Mexican consumption.

Some economists chose to shrug off the retail sales data, which showed an unexpected decline of 0.4 percent in November and 1.9 percent in December, arguing that Mexicans are shopping in informal "mom-and-pop" stores not measured by the National Statistics Institute survey.

They noted that wholesale sales jumped 2.6 percent and 9.2 percent in the same months. Also, gross domestic product in the fourth quarter jumped 7.6 percent, its highest quarterly rise since 1981, and they argued that a revival in consumption, if only moderate, partly contributed to that.

Thorne said there may have been some switch among the poor to small corner stores, and toward buying food in bulk at large distribution centers. But he said the majority of shopping was done via retailers, and there the picture remained patchy.
"The fact is, there is still a credit crunch, there are falling real wages and consumers were still vulnerable to price increases in December," he said.

Countering arguments that a surge in consumer imports late last year also suggested spending was on the rebound, he noted that they remain some 20 percent below their level in 1994, before the peso crisis -- as are retail sales levels.

He explained the surge in wholesale sales as a result of what he called "inter-enterprise" business, to firms profiting from the economic recovery rather than to households that have been left behind.

Sergio Martin, economist at ING Barings, also pointed to a slump in sales reported by the National Association of Department Stores (ANTAD) in December as further evidence that "consumption is not in good shape."

He said central bank officials had sought to play down the ANTAD numbers, but anecdotally, he said, they were borne out by large retailers. "What I have heard from companies in the stock market is that sales in December were not good. If they don't know what they're talking about, nobody does," he said.
An ING Barings report last month noted that while employment was rising, wages had failed to improve up to October, and Martin said that trend continued into November.

"More disappointing still is that among wage earners there appears to be downward mobility," the report said. In 1994, it estimated 45.9 percent of the population earned from one to two times the minimum wage, a level that had jumped to 53.7 percent in 1996. "In contrast, the number of workers earning greater multiples of the minimum wage has declined."
Low wages, depressed consumer confidence and high debt levels left over from the crisis were keeping the lid on consumption, he said.
Moreover, he explained the sharper-than-expected rise in Q4 GDP as being partly due to statistical comparisons with downwardly revised Q4 data in 1995.
"The figures from retail sales show consumption is recovering, but not as much as the GDP indicates," he said.
